text: Varna (1 point) compares the temperament class of the two Moon signs and gives the point when the first side's class is the same or higher.

Varna koota sorts the twelve Moon signs into four temperament classes: Brahmin (Karka, Vrishchika, Meena), Kshatriya (Mesha, Simha, Dhanu), Vaishya (Vrishabha, Kanya, Makara) and Shudra (Mithuna, Tula, Kumbha). The single point is given when the first side's class is the same as or above the second's, and withheld otherwise. It is the lightest of the eight kootas and is read for how the two temperaments sit together in everyday matters, not for anything about family or background.

Varna koota is the first and smallest of the Ashtakoota, worth 1 of the 36 points. The Muhurta Chintamani groups the Moon signs by element into four classes named after the old social orders but used here only as temperaments: water signs (Karka, Vrishchika, Meena) are Brahmin, read as reflective; fire signs (Mesha, Simha, Dhanu) are Kshatriya, read as assertive; earth signs (Vrishabha, Kanya, Makara) are Vaishya, read as practical; air signs (Mithuna, Tula, Kumbha) are Shudra, read as adaptable. The point is given when the first side's class is equal to or higher than the second side's in this order, and is withheld when it is lower. Because the ordering is one-directional, swapping the two profiles can change the point; this app follows the Drik Panchang convention of placing the vara (groom) side first. A missing Varna point is never read on its own; it is one point among thirty-six, and the summary weighs the whole.
Vashya (2 points) compares the vashya class of the two Moon signs and scores 2 for the same class, less for friendly classes and 0 for hostile ones.

Vashya koota groups the Moon signs into five classes: Chatushpada (four-footed), Manava (human), Jalachara (water-dwelling), Vanachara (wild) and Keeta (insect). Dhanu counts as Manava in its first half and Chatushpada in its second; Makara is Chatushpada in its first half and Jalachara in its second. The full 2 points go to the same class, 1 or a half to classes the table calls friendly, and 0 to pairs it calls hostile. It is read for mutual influence, whether each side can draw the other along.

Vashya koota, worth 2 of 36 points, asks whether the two Moon signs belong to classes that naturally pull in the same direction. The classes are Chatushpada (Mesha, Vrishabha, the second half of Dhanu, the first half of Makara), Manava (Mithuna, Kanya, Tula, Kumbha, the first half of Dhanu), Jalachara (Karka, Meena, the second half of Makara), Vanachara (Simha) and Keeta (Vrishchika). The split signs follow the Muhurta Chintamani and match Drik Panchang's scoring, so the Moon's exact degree matters for Dhanu and Makara. The table gives 2 points when both Moons share a class, 1 point for most mixed pairs, a half point for Chatushpada with Vanachara or Manava with Jalachara, and 0 for Manava with Vanachara, Vanachara with Keeta, or Keeta with Vanachara. The classical reading is of attraction and influence: a full score suggests the two are easily led by each other, a zero suggests each keeps a separate pull. Like every koota it is read inside the total of 36, never alone.
Tara (3 points) counts each birth nakshatra from the other and gives 1½ points per direction when the remainder is not 3, 5 or 7.

Tara koota counts from the first side's birth nakshatra to the second side's, and then the other way round, dividing each count by nine and keeping the remainder. A remainder of 3 (Vipat), 5 (Pratyari) or 7 (Vadha) is an unfavourable tara for that direction; any other remainder, including 0 read as 9, is favourable. Each favourable direction earns 1½ points, so the koota gives 3, 1½ or 0. It is read for the day-to-day ease between the two, using the same nine taras as the daily Tara bala.

Tara koota, worth 3 of 36 points, applies the nine-tara cycle used for daily Tara bala to the two birth nakshatras. Counting from the first side's nakshatra to the second's (inclusive) and dividing by nine gives a remainder from 1 to 9: Janma (1), Sampat (2), Vipat (3), Kshema (4), Pratyari (5), Sadhaka (6), Vadha (7), Mitra (8) and Param Mitra (9). The count is then repeated from the second side to the first. The Muhurta Chintamani counts Vipat, Pratyari and Vadha as the unfavourable taras, so a direction landing on 3, 5 or 7 earns nothing and every other direction earns 1½. Both directions favourable gives the full 3 points, one favourable gives 1½, neither gives 0. Because the two counts are not mirror images, the result can differ between the two directions, which the Why? sheet shows as two separate tara names. The koota is read for everyday compatibility and mutual well-being, and a low score here is one ingredient of the total, not a verdict.
Yoni (4 points) compares the animal symbol of the two birth nakshatras: 4 for the same animal, 2 for neutral pairs, 1 for unfriendly pairs and 0 for sworn enemies.

Yoni koota assigns each of the 27 nakshatras one of fourteen animal symbols: horse, elephant, sheep, snake, dog, cat, rat, cow, buffalo, tiger, deer, monkey, mongoose and lion. The same animal on both sides earns the full 4 points, a neutral pair 2, an unfriendly pair 1, and the classical sworn-enemy pairs (such as cat and rat, snake and mongoose, cow and tiger) 0. It is read for instinctive and physical compatibility, the comfort two people feel in close company.

Yoni koota, worth 4 of 36 points, uses the animal symbol the Muhurta Chintamani gives each nakshatra: Ashwini and Shatabhisha horse, Bharani and Revati elephant, Krittika and Pushya sheep, Rohini and Mrigashira snake, Ardra and Mula dog, Punarvasu and Ashlesha cat, Magha and Purva Phalguni rat, Uttara Phalguni and Uttara Bhadrapada cow, Hasta and Swati buffalo, Chitra and Vishakha tiger, Anuradha and Jyeshtha deer, Purva Ashadha and Shravana monkey, Uttara Ashadha mongoose, Dhanishta and Purva Bhadrapada lion. The same animal earns 4 points. This app uses a four-level table: neutral pairs 2 points, unfriendly pairs 1, and the sworn-enemy pairs 0 (horse and buffalo, elephant and lion, sheep and monkey, snake and mongoose, dog and deer, cat and rat, cow and tiger). Drik Panchang grades some friendly pairs 3 with a finer five-level table this app could not source, so a few pairs differ from it by one point; those are documented in the reference notes. The koota is read for instinctive ease between the two, inside the total of 36.
Graha Maitri (5 points) compares the lords of the two Moon signs by Parashara's natural friendships, from 5 for friends or the same lord down to 0 for mutual enemies.

Graha Maitri koota looks at the planets ruling the two Moon signs and asks how they regard each other in Parashara's table of natural friendships. The same lord, or two lords who are mutual friends, earns the full 5 points; a friend on one side and a neutral on the other 4; two neutrals 3; a friend on one side and an enemy on the other 1; a neutral and an enemy a half point; two mutual enemies 0. It is read for mental outlook and the ease of understanding each other's way of thinking.

Graha Maitri koota, worth 5 of 36 points, compares the lords of the two Moon signs (Sun for Simha, Moon for Karka, Mars for Mesha and Vrishchika, Mercury for Mithuna and Kanya, Jupiter for Dhanu and Meena, Venus for Vrishabha and Tula, Saturn for Makara and Kumbha) using Parashara's natural friendships, the same table the chart's dignity tags use. Each lord's view of the other is taken separately: the Sun counts Moon, Mars and Jupiter as friends and Venus and Saturn as enemies; the Moon counts Sun and Mercury as friends and no planet as enemy; Mars counts Sun, Moon and Jupiter as friends and Mercury as enemy; Mercury counts Sun and Venus as friends and the Moon as enemy; Jupiter counts Sun, Moon and Mars as friends and Mercury and Venus as enemies; Venus counts Mercury and Saturn as friends and Sun and Moon as enemies; Saturn counts Mercury and Venus as friends and Sun, Moon and Mars as enemies. The two views combine into the score: 5 for the same lord or mutual friendship, 4 for friend with neutral, 3 for mutual neutrality, 1 for friend with enemy, a half point for neutral with enemy, 0 for mutual enmity. It is read for how the two minds meet, inside the total of 36.
Gana (6 points) compares the gana of the two birth nakshatras: 6 for the same gana, 5 for Deva with Manushya, 1 for Manushya with Rakshasa, 0 for Deva with Rakshasa.

Gana koota sorts the 27 nakshatras into three ganas, Deva, Manushya and Rakshasa, old names that the tradition uses for three dispositions: gentle, practical and forceful. The same gana on both sides earns 6 points, Deva with Manushya 5, Manushya with Rakshasa 1, and Deva with Rakshasa 0. It is one of the heavier kootas and is read for basic disposition, how the two react under pressure and whether their natural tempos match. The names describe styles, not people.

Gana koota, worth 6 of 36 points, uses the three-fold grouping of the nakshatras given in the Muhurta Chintamani. Deva gana: Ashwini, Mrigashira, Punarvasu, Pushya, Hasta, Swati, Anuradha, Shravana, Revati. Manushya gana: Bharani, Rohini, Ardra, Purva Phalguni, Uttara Phalguni, Purva Ashadha, Uttara Ashadha, Purva Bhadrapada, Uttara Bhadrapada. Rakshasa gana: Krittika, Ashlesha, Magha, Chitra, Vishakha, Jyeshtha, Mula, Dhanishta, Shatabhisha. The scores are 6 for the same gana, 5 for Deva with Manushya (in either order), 1 for Manushya with Rakshasa and 0 for Deva with Rakshasa; this app does not apply the lower one-directional variants some almanacs use, so the result is the same whichever profile is placed first. The three names are read as dispositions, mild, worldly and intense, rather than as any judgement of a person, and the koota is read for how two temperaments settle into one household. As with the other kootas it contributes to the 36-point total and is weighed there.
Bhakoot (7 points) counts the sign distance between the two Moons and gives all 7 unless the pair is 2/12, 5/9 or 6/8 apart or shares one nakshatra pada.

Bhakoot koota counts how many signs apart the two Moons stand, in both directions. Pairs that are 2 and 12, 5 and 9, or 6 and 8 apart are called Bhakoot dosha and score 0; every other distance, including the same sign, scores the full 7. Two Moons in the same nakshatra and the same pada also score 0 by convention. It is the second-heaviest koota and is read for shared direction in family life and provision. The exceptions that some traditions allow are named on the dosha row.

Bhakoot koota, worth 7 of 36 points, is scored from the mutual sign distance of the two Moons. Counting from the first side's Moon sign to the second's and back, the pairs 2/12 (dwirdwadasha), 5/9 (navapanchama) and 6/8 (shadashtaka) are the three Bhakoot doshas and score 0; distances of 1/1, 3/11, 4/10 and 7/7 score the full 7. The tradition reads 2/12 for strain over resources, 5/9 for strain over children and shared aims, and 6/8 for health and separation, always as themes to be aware of rather than events. This app follows Drik Panchang's convention: the same-lord exception (Mesha–Vrishchika, Vrishabha–Tula, Mithuna–Kanya, Dhanu–Meena, Makara–Kumbha) is named on the dosha row so a pandit can weigh it, but it is not added back into the score, and two Moons in the same nakshatra and pada score 0 even when the sign distance is fine. The Why? inputs give the distance, whether the dosha applies and which exception, if any, is relevant. Bhakoot is weighed inside the total with Nadi, the other heavy koota.
Nadi (8 points) compares the nadi of the two birth nakshatras: 8 for different nadis, 0 for the same nadi unless an exception lifts it.

Nadi koota assigns each nakshatra to one of three nadis, Adi, Madhya and Antya, in a repeating pattern around the zodiac. Different nadis on the two sides earn the full 8 points; the same nadi is Nadi dosha and earns 0, unless both Moons are in the same sign with different nakshatras, or in the same nakshatra with different padas, in which case the dosha is lifted and the full points given. It is the heaviest koota and is traditionally read for constitution and the well-being of the line.

Nadi koota, worth 8 of 36 points, is the heaviest of the Ashtakoota. The 27 nakshatras are laid out in a zigzag of three nadis: Adi (Ashwini, Ardra, Punarvasu, Uttara Phalguni, Hasta, Jyeshtha, Mula, Shatabhisha, Purva Bhadrapada), Madhya (Bharani, Mrigashira, Pushya, Purva Phalguni, Chitra, Anuradha, Purva Ashadha, Dhanishta, Uttara Bhadrapada) and Antya (Krittika, Rohini, Ashlesha, Magha, Swati, Vishakha, Uttara Ashadha, Shravana, Revati). Different nadis earn the full 8; the same nadi is Nadi dosha and earns 0. The Muhurta Chintamani and later almanacs allow two exceptions, both applied here and matching Drik Panchang: if the two Moons are in the same sign but different nakshatras, or in the same nakshatra but different padas, the dosha is lifted and 8 points are given; the same nakshatra and the same pada keeps the dosha. The traditional reading links the nadis to the three humours of Ayurveda and reads a shared nadi for strain on constitution and progeny; this app presents it as a classical rule to weigh, not as a medical statement. The row names the two nadis and any exception that applied.

Nadi dosha is lifted in this pairing because both Moons stand in the same sign while their nakshatras differ. The Muhurta Chintamani and the common almanac practice treat a shared Moon sign as outweighing a shared nadi, so the full 8 points are given and the dosha row names the exception instead of the dosha. Drik Panchang applies the same exception, which is why this app's total matches its reference pairs. The inputs list both Moon signs and both nakshatras so the condition can be checked by hand.

Nadi dosha is lifted in this pairing because both Moons stand in the same nakshatra while their padas differ. The tradition holds that two births under one star are joined more closely than the shared nadi divides them, provided the pada is not also the same; when nakshatra and pada both match, the dosha stays. The full 8 points are given and the row names this exception. The inputs show the two nakshatras and padas so the distinction between same-pada and different-pada is visible.

The two Moon signs in this pairing fall at a Bhakoot dosha distance but share one ruling planet: Mesha and Vrishchika (Mars), Vrishabha and Tula (Venus), Mithuna and Kanya (Mercury), Dhanu and Meena (Jupiter), or Makara and Kumbha (Saturn). Many traditions treat a shared lord as lifting the dosha. This app names the exception on the row so it can be weighed, but follows Drik Panchang in not adding the 7 points back, so the printed total matches that reference. A pandit may choose to count it; the row makes the choice visible.

Bhakoot scores 0 in this pairing although the sign distance itself carries no dosha, because both Moons stand in the same nakshatra and the same pada. This eka-nakshatra eka-pada convention, used by Drik Panchang and several almanacs, reads two Moons at effectively one point of the zodiac as too alike for the Bhakoot points, and the matching reference pairs this app was checked against follow it. The row shows the shared nakshatra and pada; Nadi is scored separately by its own rule.
